implementation_notes: TypeScript compiles to JavaScript and has no inline keyword and no runtime of its own, so the engine's inlining rules are the JavaScript ones and the lever is shape stability, not annotation: monomorphic call sites and consistent object shapes. TypeScript's contribution is the type system making the hot path monomorphic by construction - a union type at a call site becomes a megamorphic property access at runtime, and narrowing it or splitting the branch makes it monomorphic. So 'inlining' in TypeScript is really 'keep the call site monomorphic': split a union-typed property access with a typeof or instanceof guard, or use a discriminated union so the engine sees one shape per branch. Manual inlining by copying a body is discouraged: it removes the function the engine could have optimised as a unit and duplicates the logic.
idiom_name: no keyword; JS-engine inlining with shape stability - narrow union types and discriminated unions to keep call sites monomorphic
pitfalls: TypeScript has no inline keyword and no runtime; it emits the same JS, so the engine's inlining and shape rules apply unchanged.
A union-typed property access or call is megamorphic at runtime and defeats the inline cache; narrow it or use a discriminated union.
Copying a function body manually removes the identity the engine could optimise and duplicates the logic; fix the type/shape instead.
An `any`-typed value at a hot site is effectively a megamorphic access - the type annotation is the lever here, not the runtime.
Inlining happens in the optimised tier, so a one-shot micro-benchmark of a hot function does not reflect the steady-state inlined code.
